paras: The mob attack on the Looker building took place in Moline, Illinois, on the night of 15 August 1910, when about 50 white men, many armed, surrounded a building said to house about 100 Black residents and smashed its windows with rocks. The crowd had gathered after a report that two Black men had pursued a white girl, and three police officers dispersed it before anyone was reported hurt. The Rock Island Argus presented the night as a narrowly averted "race clash," and a wire item carried a larger version of it as far as Spokane.

The Looker building, at Twenty-fourth avenue and Fifteenth street, was a large three-story former business block that had been converted into a dwelling. According to the Argus, "various insults to white people" had been reported in the neighborhood, and white residents had made "verbal threats of prosecution." The paper later wrote that Moline was "overrun by negroes" brought in by contractors with large building jobs in the city.

On the evening of 15 August a report spread that two Black men had pursued a white girl and beaten two young men who tried to protect her. Between 11 and 12 o'clock about 50 men, some mounted and most of them armed, gathered around the Looker building, "prepared to 'regulate'" the first Black man who showed himself. Rocks were thrown through the building's windows, but no occupant came out. Three police officers soon arrived and dispersed the crowd "before any further harm had been done."

No report of arrests, either of members of the crowd or of the accused men, was found. On 20 August the Argus reported that Tom Bradley, a 60-year-old Black resident of 40 years who lived in a building called the "Incubator," had spent a week in the county jail at his own request, saying whites were about to lynch him. Bradley was committed to the insane hospital at Watertown; the police had discounted his warning of a race riot, though the paper noted a rumor that he had received "advance notice" of the clash.

When two Black men shot and killed Edward Wyman during a holdup in Moline on 3 September, the Argus recalled that a "party of indignant citizens" had organized at midnight a few weeks earlier and "went gunning for the offenders," crediting the police with preventing a race clash.

Only white papers covered the episode, and no Black-press report of it was found. The Rock Island Argus ran the story on its front page under the headline "Moline Is Close to a Race Clash," called the gathering an "Uprising" in its subheads, and called the white men a "mob." The Argus treated the charge against the two Black men as a "report" and a "rumored attack," but it led with the white girl and with complaints of insults to white people.

A one-sentence wire item in the Spokane Press on 22 August stated as fact that five Black men had "attacked a white girl" and said a hundred white residents of South Moline were hunting them. By the Argus's September account, the episode had become background in a murder report that described the city as "overrun by negroes" imported by contractors.

The local and wire versions differ: the Argus gave two accused men, about 50 in the crowd, and no one seized, while the Spokane Press gave five accused, a hundred hunters, and "several negroes" rescued by police from lynching. The Argus account was local and published the next day, while the Spokane item appeared a week later as a brief wire summary.

reader.title: Mob attack on the Looker building, Moline, Illinois
bases: An armed crowd of about 50 white men surrounded and stoned a building said to house about 100 Black residents, aiming at whoever showed himself rather than at named individuals (A1, A5).

The local Rock Island Argus (A1, recalled in A4/A5) and an independent wire item in the Spokane Press (A3) agree that a white crowd gathered against Black residents of Moline after a report about a white girl and that police intervened, though they differ on numbers and on whether anyone was seized.

accounts.label: Local report (Rock Island Argus)
accounts.gist: About 50 men, many armed, gathered at the Looker building after a report that two Black men had pursued a white girl and beaten her defenders; they stoned the windows, no occupant appeared, and three police officers dispersed them.

accounts.label: Wire report
accounts.gist: A hundred white residents of South Moline were hunting five Black men said to have attacked a white girl, and police had already rescued several Black men from lynching.

framing.detail: The Argus called the gathering a 'mob' that police dispersed but headlined a near 'Race Clash' and 'Uprising', gave the white girl's report and 'insults to white people' as the cause, and later blamed Black workers 'imported by contractors'.
The Spokane Press ran a one-sentence wire item stating as fact that five Black men 'attacked a white girl' and that police had rescued several from lynching.

info: Night of 15 August 1910, between 11 and 12 o'clock ('last night' in the 16 August paper)

The Looker building, Twenty-fourth avenue and Fifteenth street, Moline; a former business building converted into a dwelling, three stories, said to house fully 100 Black residents. The wire item places the crowd in South Moline.
No one was reported hurt; the Argus says no occupant appeared. The wire item says police rescued 'several negroes' from lynching.

A report that a white girl had been pursued by two Black men, who then beat two young men who interfered to protect her (A1, A5); the wire item says five Black men 'attacked' a white girl (A3). The Argus also cites earlier 'various insults to white people' in the neighborhood.
White men of the neighborhood, described as a 'mob' and as 'a party of indignant citizens'; none named.
